label: thm:main
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:main}
Let \(X\) be a smooth connected projective variety of dimension \(n\geq1\), and let \(L_1,\ldots,L_n\) be nef line bundles. Put \(x_i=c_1(L_i)\in H^2(X;\mathbb Z)\). Suppose that the cohomology ring, top intersection, and first Chern class satisfy
  
\[
\begin{gathered}
H^*(X;\mathbb Z)\cong\frac{\mathbb Z[x_1,\ldots,x_n]}{(x_1^2,\ldots,x_n^2)},\\
\int_Xx_1\cdots x_n=1,\qquad c_1(TX)=2\sum_{i=1}^n x_i.
\end{gathered}
\]
  
Then there is an algebraic isomorphism
  
\[
\Phi:X\xrightarrow{\ \cong\ }(\mathbb P^1)^n,
\qquad
L_i\cong\Phi^*\operatorname{pr}_i^*
\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(1)\quad(1\leq i\leq n).
\]
  
Each \(L_i\) is generated by its global sections and \(\dim_{\mathbb C}H^0(X,L_i)=2\). For any choice of basis \(s_{i,0},s_{i,1}\in H^0(X,L_i)\), the map
  
\[
p\longmapsto
\bigl([s_{1,0}(p):s_{1,1}(p)],\ldots,
[s_{n,0}(p):s_{n,1}(p)]\bigr)
\]
  
is an isomorphism with the property.
head: environment

label: def:htw
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:htw}
An action of \(\mathbb C^{\times}\) on a smooth connected projective variety satisfies the \emph{HTW condition} if it is effective, its fixed locus is nonempty and finite, and every weight of its tangent representation at every fixed point is \(1\) or \(-1\).
head: environment

label: thm:graph
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:graph}
Let \(X\) satisfy the HTW condition, with fixed points labelled as in Theorem~\ref{thm:htw}. Suppose that every minimal directed edge has the form
  
\[
p_I\longrightarrow p_{I\cup\{j\}},\qquad j\notin I.
\]
  
Then every Hattori line bundle is nef. The isomorphism in Theorem~\ref{thm:main} can be chosen to be equivariant for the action
  
\[
t\cdot([z_{1,0}:z_{1,1}],\ldots,[z_{n,0}:z_{n,1}])
=([tz_{1,0}:z_{1,1}],\ldots,[tz_{n,0}:z_{n,1}]).
\]
head: environment

label: lem:semifree
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:semifree}
If the action satisfies the HTW condition, then it is free outside its fixed locus.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let \(x\in X\) be a point which is not fixed. Its stabiliser is a finite cyclic group \(\boldsymbol\mu_d=\{t\in\mathbb C^{\times}:t^d=1\}\), and we must show that \(d=1\). Suppose that \(d>1\) and choose \(\zeta\in\boldsymbol\mu_d\) with \(\zeta\ne1\). As \(\mathbb C^{\times}\) is abelian, \(\zeta\) fixes the orbit of \(x\) pointwise, and hence its closure, which contains the fixed point
  
\[
p=\lim_{t\to0}t\cdot x.
\]
  
All tangent weights at \(p\) are \(\pm1\), so \(\zeta\) acts on \(T_pX\) with eigenvalues \(\zeta^{\pm1}\), neither of which is one. Since a finite-order automorphism can be linearised near a fixed point, \(p\) is an isolated point of \(X^{\zeta}\). This contradicts the fact that \(X^{\zeta}\) contains the orbit closure through \(p\).
head: environment

label: thm:htw
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:htw}
Let \(X\) satisfy the HTW condition. The following statements hold.
\begin{enumerate}[(i),noitemsep]
\item There are exactly \(\binom nk\) fixed points \(p\) with \(\lambda(p)=k\).  In particular, \(X\) has \(2^n\) fixed points.
\item The fixed points can be labelled by subsets \(I\subset\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and \(\lambda(p_I)=|I|.\)
\item There are integral classes \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\in H^2(X;\mathbb Z)\) such that
  
\[
H^*(X;\mathbb Z)
\cong
\frac{\mathbb Z[x_1,\ldots,x_n]}
{(x_1^2,\ldots,x_n^2)},
\qquad
\int_Xx_1\cdots x_n=1.
\]
  
\item The total Chern class is \(c(TX)=\prod_{i=1}^n(1+2x_i)\). In particular, the first Chern class is
  
\[
c_1(TX)=2(x_1+\cdots+x_n).
\]
  
\item With the generator \(u\) fixed above, the classes \(x_i\) have equivariant lifts \(a_i\in H^2_{\mathbb C^{\times}}(X;\mathbb Z)\) satisfying
  
\[
a_i|_{p_I}=
\begin{cases}
-u,&i\in I,\\
0,&i\notin I,
\end{cases}
\]
  
with the convention that \(p_{\varnothing}\) is the point with all tangent weights positive.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

label: prop:f2
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:f2}
The surface \(\mathbb F_2\) admits a \(\mathbb C^{\times}\)-action satisfying the HTW condition, but
  
\[
\mathbb F_2\not\cong\mathbb P^1\times\mathbb P^1.
\]
  
Moreover, its cohomology has generators \(x_1,x_2\) satisfying all the ordinary-cohomology and Chern-class relations in Theorem~\ref{thm:htw}, while \(x_2\) is not nef.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let \(\mathbb C^{\times}\) act on the base by \(t\cdot[z_0:z_1]=[tz_0:z_1]\), with fixed points \(0=[0:1]\) and \(\infty=[1:0]\) of tangent weights \(1\) and \(-1\), respectively. We give the trivial summand \(\mathcal O\) the constant fibre weight \(-1\), and we linearise \(\mathcal O(2)\) with fibre weights \(0\) over \(0\) and \(-2\) over \(\infty\). The induced action on the projective bundle has four fixed points, namely the summand lines in the two fixed fibres. Writing \(E=\mathcal O\oplus\mathcal O(2)\), the vertical tangent space at a line \(\ell\subset E_b\) is \(\operatorname{Hom}(\ell,E_b/\ell)\), whose weight is the weight of \(E_b/\ell\) minus that of \(\ell\). This gives the following table.
  
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}
\text{fixed point}
&\text{base weight}
&\text{vertical weight}
&\text{tangent weights}\\ \hline
(0,[\mathcal O])&1&0-(-1)=1&(1,1)\\
(0,[\mathcal O(2)])&1&-1-0=-1&(1,-1)\\
(\infty,[\mathcal O])&-1&-2-(-1)=-1&(-1,-1)\\
(\infty,[\mathcal O(2)])&-1&-1-(-2)=1&(-1,1).
\end{array}
\]
  
Every tangent weight is therefore \(\pm1\), and the action is effective because it is effective on the base, so the HTW condition holds.

Let \(S\subset\mathbb F_2\) be the section given by the subbundle \(\mathcal O(2)\), and let \(F\) be a fibre. The normal bundle of \(S\) is \(\operatorname{Hom}(\mathcal O(2),\mathcal O)\cong\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(-2)\), so
  
\[
S^2=-2,
\qquad S\cdot F=1,
\qquad F^2=0.
\]
  
On \(\mathbb P^1\times\mathbb P^1\) every effective curve has class \(aH_1+bH_2\) with \(a,b\geq0\), and hence self-intersection \(2ab\geq0\). The curve \(S\) therefore shows that \(\mathbb F_2\) is not isomorphic to the product.

Writing \(S\) and \(F\) also for their classes in \(H^2(\mathbb F_2;\mathbb Z)\), the projective bundle formula gives
  
\[
H^*(\mathbb F_2;\mathbb Z)
\cong
\frac{\mathbb Z[S,F]}{(F^2,S^2+2SF)},
\]
  
and the classes \(x_1=F\) and \(x_2=S+F\) satisfy
  
\[
x_1^2=x_2^2=0,
\qquad
\int_{\mathbb F_2}x_1x_2=1.
\]
  
To find the canonical class, write \(K_{\mathbb F_2}=aS+bF\). The adjunction formula \cite[Chapter V, Proposition 1.5]{Hr-Al77} on a fibre gives \(K_{\mathbb F_2}\cdot F=-2\), so \(a=-2\). On \(S\cong\mathbb P^1\) it gives \((K_{\mathbb F_2}+S)\cdot S=-2\), so \(K_{\mathbb F_2}\cdot S=0\) and \(b=-4\). Hence \(-K_{\mathbb F_2}=2S+4F\) and
  
\[
c_1(T\mathbb F_2)=2(x_1+x_2).
\]
  
Since \(\mathbb F_2\) is a \(\mathbb P^1\)-bundle over \(\mathbb P^1\), its Euler characteristic is four, and as \(x_1x_2\) has integral one we get
  
\[
c(T\mathbb F_2)=1+2(x_1+x_2)+4x_1x_2=(1+2x_1)(1+2x_2).
\]
  
These are the same identities as on the product. However, the second class has negative degree on the section,
  
\[
x_2\cdot S=(S+F)\cdot S=-1,
\]
  
so \(x_2\) is not nef. The anticanonical class also has degree zero on this curve,
  
\[
(-K_{\mathbb F_2})\cdot S=(2S+4F)\cdot S=0.
\]
  
An ample line bundle has strictly positive degree on every curve.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: One might instead ask whether it is enough for some positive combination of the Hattori classes to be ample. The same example shows that it is not. If \(a,b\in\mathbb Z\) with \(a>0\) and \(b>2a\), then the line bundle \(\mathcal O_{\mathbb F_2}(aS+bF)\) has first Chern class \(aS+bF=(b-a)x_1+ax_2\), a positive combination of the two HTW generators, and it is ample. To see this, put \(A=aS+bF\). Then \(A^2=2a(b-a)>0\) and \(A\cdot S=b-2a>0\). Any other curve \(C\), of class \(cS+dF\), satisfies \(c=C\cdot F\geq0\) because the fibre class is nef, and \(d-2c=C\cdot S\geq0\) because distinct integral curves on a surface meet non-negatively. As \((c,d)\neq(0,0)\), we get \(A\cdot C=ad+(b-2a)c>0\), and the Nakai-Moishezon criterion \cite[Theorem 1.2.23]{La-Po04} shows that \(A\) is ample. So the total class can be ample even though \(x_2\) is not nef, and the hypothesis in Theorem~\ref{thm:main} has to concern the individual factor classes.
head: environment

label: thm:nef-complexity
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:nef-complexity}
Let \((Y,B+M)\) be a generalised klt log Calabi-Yau pair, where \(Y\) is a normal projective variety of dimension \(n\geq1\). Suppose that \(D_1,\ldots,D_r\) are numerically nonzero nef Cartier divisors on \(Y\), and that \(b_1,\ldots,b_r\) are positive real numbers satisfying
  
\[
M=\sum_{j=1}^r b_jD_j.
\]
  
Assume that \(B+M\) is big. Let \(W\) be the real span of the numerical divisor classes, and write \(\sigma\) for its dimension,
  
\[
W=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}\{[D_1],\ldots,[D_r]\}
\subseteq N^1(Y)_{\mathbb R},
\qquad
\sigma=\dim_{\mathbb R}W.
\]
  
Then the coefficient sum satisfies
  
\[
\sum_{j=1}^r b_j\leq\min\{n+\sigma,2n\}.
\]
  
If this bound is attained, all the following conclusions hold.
\begin{enumerate}[(i),noitemsep]
\item The numerical span satisfies \(n+\sigma\leq2n\).

\item There are positive integers \(d_1,\ldots,d_{\ell}\), with \(\sum_{k=1}^{\ell}d_k=n\), and an algebraic isomorphism
  
\[
\Psi:Y\xrightarrow{\ \cong\ }\prod_{k=1}^{\ell}\mathbb P^{d_k}.
\]
  
Write \(\operatorname{pr}_k\) for projection onto the \(k\)-th factor.

\item The boundary vanishes, and the decomposition is numerically anticanonical,
  
\[
B=0,
\qquad
K_Y+\sum_{j=1}^r b_jD_j\equiv0.
\]
  

\item Each divisor represents a factor hyperplane bundle. More precisely, for every \(j\in\{1,\ldots,r\}\), there is an index \(k(j)\in\{1,\ldots,\ell\}\) such that
  
\[
\mathcal O_Y(D_j)
\cong
\Psi^*\operatorname{pr}_{k(j)}^*
\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{d_{k(j)}}}(1).
\]
  
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

label: thm:classification
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:classification}
Let \(Y\) be a smooth connected projective variety of dimension \(n\geq1\). Let \(D_1,\ldots,D_r\) be nef Cartier divisors which are not numerically trivial, and let \(b_1,\ldots,b_r\in\mathbb Q_{>0}\). Suppose that
  
\[
-K_Y\equiv M:=\sum_{j=1}^r b_jD_j,
\qquad M\text{ is big},
\qquad \sum_{j=1}^r b_j=2n.
\]
  
Then \(Y\cong(\mathbb P^1)^n\).
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let
  
\[
W=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}([D_1],\ldots,[D_r])
\subseteq N^1(Y)_{\mathbb R},
\qquad \sigma=\dim_{\mathbb R}W.
\]
  
By the discussion above, \((Y,0+M)\) is a generalised klt log Calabi-Yau pair, so Theorem~4.2 of \cite{EnFiGoMoSvWaWa-Ne25} gives
  
\[
2n=\sum_{j=1}^r b_j\leq\min(n+\sigma,2n),
\]
  
and therefore \(\sigma\geq n\). Theorem \ref{thm:nef-complexity} above of now gives \(\sigma\leq n\), an isomorphism with the  product \(Y\cong\prod_{k=1}^{\ell}\mathbb P^{d_k}\), and identify each of the \(D_j\) with a factor hyperplane class. Every factor must occur among these classes, for otherwise \(\sum_j b_jD_j\) would have degree zero on a line in the missing factor, where \(-K_Y\) has degree \(d_k+1>0\). Consequently \(\ell=\sigma=n\), and since \(\sum_kd_k=n\) with every \(d_k\geq1\), all the \(d_k\) are one.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: Under a Fano hypothesis, Theorem~1.6 of the same paper gives the coefficient bound and the product conclusion directly, and in our application \(X\) is shown to be Fano before the classification is used (Lemma~\ref{lem:fano}). We keep the formulation via Theorem~4.2 because it needs only a nef and big anticanonical decomposition.
head: environment

label: lem:intersections
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:intersections}
The divisors \(D_i\) are nef and numerically nonzero, their numerical classes are independent, and
  
\[
D^n=n!,\qquad -K_X\equiv2D.
\]
  
In fact \(\rho(X)=n\).
head: environment

label: eq:dual-intersections
title: Proof
body_md:
The \(D_i\) are nef because the \(L_i\) are. For \(1\leq i,j\leq n\), the relations \(x_i^2=0\) and \(\int_Xx_1\cdots x_n=1\) give
\refstepcounter{equation}
  
\[
\tag{\theequation}
\label{eq:dual-intersections}
D_i\prod_{k\ne j}D_k
=\begin{cases}1,&i=j,\\0,&i\ne j,\end{cases}
\]
  
where for \(n=1\) the empty product is the fundamental cycle \([X]\). Pairing a relation \(\sum_ia_i[D_i]=0\) with the one-cycle \(\prod_{k\ne j}D_k\) gives \(a_j=0\), so the classes \([D_i]\) are independent and in particular nonzero. Since \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) is a basis of \(H^2(X;\mathbb Z)\), every line bundle \(L\) has \(c_1(L)=\sum_ia_ix_i\) with \(a_i\in\mathbb Z\), and then \(L\equiv\sum_ia_iD_i\). Thus the \([D_i]\) span \(N^1(X)_{\mathbb R}\) and \(\rho(X)=n\). In the expansion of \(D^n\) every monomial with a repeated index vanishes, and each of the remaining \(n!\) monomials equals one, so \(D^n=n!\). Finally,
  
\[
c_1(-K_X)=c_1(TX)=2\sum_i x_i
=c_1\!\left(\bigotimes_iL_i^{\otimes2}\right),
\]
  
which gives \(-K_X\equiv2D\).
head: environment

label: lem:big
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:big}
The anticanonical divisor is nef and big.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: As a sum of nef divisors, \(D\) is nef. Hence \(-K_X\equiv2D\) is nef, with \((-K_X)^n=2^nn!>0\) by Lemma~\ref{lem:intersections}, and \eqref{eq:nef-big} shows that it is big.
head: environment

label: lem:fano
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:fano}
For positive integers \(a_1,\ldots,a_n\), the divisor \(A=\sum_i a_iD_i\) is ample. In particular, \(D\) and \(-K_X\) are ample, and \(X\) is Fano.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Choose an ample Cartier divisor \(H\) on \(X\). By Lemma~\ref{lem:intersections} there are integers \(h_i\) with \(H\equiv\sum_ih_iD_i\), and we choose a rational number \(\varepsilon>0\) with \(a_i-\varepsilon h_i>0\) for every \(i\). Then
  
\[
A\equiv\varepsilon H+N,
\qquad
N=\sum_i(a_i-\varepsilon h_i)D_i,
\]
  
where \(N\) is nef. An ample class plus a nef class is ample \cite[Corollary 1.4.10]{La-Po04}, and ampleness only depends on the numerical class \cite[Corollary 1.2.24]{La-Po04}, so \(A\) is ample. Taking every \(a_i=1\) shows that \(D\) is ample, and hence so is \(-K_X\equiv2D\).
head: environment

label: prop:abstract-product
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:abstract-product}
There exists an algebraic isomorphism \(\psi:X\to(\mathbb P^1)^n\).
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: We apply Theorem~\ref{thm:classification} with \(r=n\), the divisors \(D_i\), and all \(b_i=2\). The \(D_i\) are nef and numerically nonzero by Lemma~\ref{lem:intersections}, the sum \(\sum_i2D_i\equiv-K_X\) is big by Lemma~\ref{lem:big}, and \(\sum_ib_i=2n=2\dim X\).
head: environment

label: lem:identify-bundles
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:identify-bundles}
After a permutation of the factors of \(P\),
  
\[
L_i\cong\psi^*H_i\qquad(1\leq i\leq n).
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Write
  
\[
B_i=(\psi^{-1})^*L_i
\cong\mathcal O(a_{i1},\ldots,a_{in}),
\qquad a_{ij}\in\mathbb Z.
\]
  
Since \(B_i\) is nef, \(a_{ij}\geq0\). For \(n\geq2\) the relation \(x_i^2=0\) becomes
  
\[
0=c_1(B_i)^2
=2\sum_{j<k}a_{ij}a_{ik}h_jh_k,
\]
  
and as the classes \(h_jh_k\) with \(j<k\) form a basis of \(H^4(P;\mathbb Z)\), at most one coefficient in each row is nonzero. This holds trivially for \(n=1\). The class \(x_i\) is primitive, since it belongs to an integral basis, so the nonzero coefficient equals one. Writing \(\sigma(i)\) for its position, we get \(B_i\cong H_{\sigma(i)}\). The map \(\sigma\) is injective because the \(x_i\) are distinct, hence it is a permutation, and permuting the factors of \(P\) gives the claim.
head: environment

label: prop:sections
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:sections}
Every \(L_i\) is globally generated with \(\dim_{\mathbb C}H^0(X,L_i)=2\). Any bases \(s_{i,0},s_{i,1}\in H^0(X,L_i)\) define morphisms
  
\[
f_i:X\longrightarrow\mathbb P^1,
\qquad f_i(p)=[s_{i,0}(p):s_{i,1}(p)],
\]
  
whose product \(\Phi=(f_1,\ldots,f_n)\) is an isomorphism and satisfies \(\Phi^*H_i\cong L_i\).
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Order the factors as in Lemma~\ref{lem:identify-bundles}. Since the other factors have only constant regular functions,
  
\[
H^0(P,H_i)=H^0(\mathbb P^1,\mathcal O(1))\cong\mathbb C^2,
\]
  
and \(H_i\) is globally generated. Pulling back by \(\psi\) gives the same properties for \(L_i\). Global generation means that \(s_{i,0}\) and \(s_{i,1}\) have no common zero, so \(f_i\) is a morphism. If the \(s_{i,a}\) are pulled back from the coordinate sections on \(P\), then \(f_i=\operatorname{pr}_i\circ\psi\) and \(\Phi=\psi\). Any other choice of bases differs by matrices \(A_i\in\operatorname{GL}_2(\mathbb C)\), and if \(a_i\) is the induced automorphism of \(\mathbb P^1\), the new map is
  
\[
(a_1\times\cdots\times a_n)\circ\psi.
\]
  
This is again an isomorphism, and since projective automorphisms preserve \(\mathcal O(1)\), it satisfies \(\Phi^*H_i\cong L_i\).
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: This is the combination of Propositions~\ref{prop:abstract-product} and \ref{prop:sections}.
head: environment

label: cor:polarised
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:polarised}
For integers \(a_1,\ldots,a_n>0\), the line bundle \(A=\bigotimes_iL_i^{\otimes a_i}\) is ample, and
  
\[
(X,A)\cong((\mathbb P^1)^n,\mathcal O(a_1,\ldots,a_n)).
\]
  
Moreover \(X\) is Fano.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Composing the Veronese embeddings of the factors given by \(\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(a_i)\) with the Segre embedding shows that \(\mathcal O(a_1,\ldots,a_n)\) is very ample, and pulling back by \(\Phi\) proves the first assertion. Since \(K_{\mathbb P^1}=\mathcal O(-2)\), we have \(-K_P=\mathcal O(2,\ldots,2)\), which is ample, so \(X\cong P\) is Fano.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md:
A \(\mathbb C^{\times}\)-\emph{linearisation} of a line bundle \(L\to X\) is an algebraic action on its total space which covers the given action on \(X\), is linear on each fibre, and it is compatible with the group action multiplication. For a fixed point \(p\), the induced representation on the one-dimensional fibre is
  
\[
t\cdot v=t^{\mu_L(p)}v,\qquad v\in L_p,
\]
  
for a unique integer \(\mu_L(p)\), called its \emph{fibre weight}. Twisting by the character \(t\mapsto t^k\) means replacing the action on the total space by \(t*v=t^k(t\cdot v)\). This adds \(k\) to every fibre weight.
head: environment

label: lem:linearisation
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:linearisation}
Every line bundle on a normal projective variety with a \(\mathbb C^{\times}\)-action admits a linearisation. If the variety is connected, any two linearisations of the same line bundle differ by a character.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Brion's linearisation theorem \cite[Theorem 2.14]{Br-Li15}, on a normal variety acted on by a connected linear algebraic group, a fixed tensor power of every line bundle is linearisable, the exponent being the stable exponent of the Picard group of the group. For \(\mathbb C^{\times}\) this exponent is one, since \(K[t,t^{-1}]\) is a principal ideal domain and so \(\operatorname{Pic}(\mathbb C^{\times}_K)=0\) for every extension field \(K\) of \(\mathbb C\). Thus the line bundle itself is linearisable.

Two linearisations differ by an invertible regular function \(r(t,p)\) on \(\mathbb C^{\times}\times X\). It is constant in \(p\), because a connected projective variety has only constant regular functions, and the group law gives \(r(st)=r(s)r(t)\) and \(r(1)=1\). Hence \(r(t)=t^k\) for some \(k\in\mathbb Z\).
head: environment

label: lem:normalise-weights
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Choose a linearisation by Lemma~\ref{lem:linearisation}, and let \(\widetilde x_i\) be the equivariant first Chern class of the associated line bundle on the Borel construction, an equivariant lift of \(x_i\). Since \(H^1(X;\mathbb Z)=0\) and \(H^*(B\mathbb C^{\times};\mathbb Z)\) vanishes in odd degrees, the Leray-Serre spectral sequence of the Borel fibration has no nonzero differentials into or out of total degree two, and it gives an exact sequence
  
\[
0\longrightarrow\mathbb Z u
\longrightarrow H^2_{\mathbb C^{\times}}(X;\mathbb Z)
\longrightarrow H^2(X;\mathbb Z)\longrightarrow0.
\]
  
As \(a_i\) and \(\widetilde x_i\) both lift \(x_i\), we have \(\widetilde x_i-a_i=k_iu\) for an integer \(k_i\). Twisting the linearisation by \(t\mapsto t^{-k_i}\) turns its equivariant first Chern class into \(a_i\). At a fixed point \(p_I\) this class restricts to \(\mu_{L_i}(p_I)u\), so the restriction formula in Theorem~\ref{thm:htw} gives \eqref{eq:normalised-weights}.
head: environment

label: lem:degree-weight
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Write \(\nu^*L\cong\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(d)\), so that \(L\cdot C=d\). The natural linearisation of \(\mathcal O(1)\) on \(\mathbb P^1\) has weights \(0\) and \(-1\) at \([0:1]\) and \([1:0]\), so \(\mathcal O(d)\) has a linearisation with weights \(0\) and \(-d\). By Lemma~\ref{lem:linearisation}, any other linearisation, in particular the pullback of that of \(L\), has weights \(k\) and \(k-d\) for some \(k\in\mathbb Z\). This proves \eqref{eq:degree-weight}. For an ample line bundle \(A\) with a linearisation it gives \(\mu_A(p)-\mu_A(q)=A\cdot C>0\), so \(p\ne q\).
head: environment

label: prop:invariant-cycles
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:invariant-cycles}
Let \(X\) be a smooth projective variety with a \(\mathbb C^{\times}\)-action. Every curve \(C\subset X\) is numerically equivalent to an effective invariant one-cycle. If the fixed locus is finite, each component of this cycle is the closure of a one-dimensional orbit.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Choose a very ample line bundle \(A\) with a linearisation (Lemma~\ref{lem:linearisation}), and let \(P_C\) be the Hilbert polynomial of \(C\) with respect to \(A\). The linearisation identifies \(t^*A\) with \(A\), so every translate \(t\cdot C\) has Hilbert polynomial \(P_C\), and the translated family over \(\mathbb C^{\times}\), being isomorphic to \(\mathbb C^{\times}\times C\), is flat. This gives a morphism
  
\[
\beta:\mathbb C^{\times}\longrightarrow
\operatorname{Hilb}_{P_C}(X),
\qquad t\longmapsto[t\cdot C].
\]
  
Since the Hilbert scheme is proper, \(\beta\) extends to \(\overline\beta:\mathbb A^1\to\operatorname{Hilb}_{P_C}(X)\), and pulling back the universal family gives a flat projective family \(\pi:\mathcal Z\to\mathbb A^1\) whose fibre \(Z_t\) is \(t\cdot C\) for \(t\ne0\). For \(s\in\mathbb C^{\times}\) the maps \(t\mapsto s\cdot\overline\beta(t)\) and \(t\mapsto\overline\beta(st)\) agree on \(\mathbb C^{\times}\), hence everywhere because the Hilbert scheme is separated, and evaluating at zero shows that \(Z_0\) is invariant.

Let \(L\) be any line bundle on \(X\). Its pullback to \(\mathcal Z\) is flat over \(\mathbb A^1\), so both \(\chi(Z_t,L|_{Z_t})\) and \(\chi(Z_t,\mathcal O_{Z_t})\) are independent of \(t\) \cite[Chapter III, Theorem 9.9]{Hr-Al77}. Let \([Z_0]_1=\sum_jm_jC_j\) be the fundamental one-cycle of the special fibre, with \(m_j\) the length of its structure sheaf at the generic point of \(C_j\). Riemann-Roch on the normalisations of the \(C_j\), together with additivity of the Euler characteristic, gives
\refstepcounter{equation}
  
\[
\tag{\theequation}
\label{eq:euler-degree}
\chi(Z_0,L|_{Z_0})-\chi(Z_0,\mathcal O_{Z_0})
=\sum_jm_j(L\cdot C_j),
\]
  
because sheaves supported at finitely many points, such as embedded points and the corrections coming from normalisation, contribute equally to both terms. The same identity at \(t=1\) gives \(L\cdot C=\chi(C,L|_C)-\chi(C,\mathcal O_C)\), and by the constancy just proved
  
\[
L\cdot C=\sum_jm_j(L\cdot C_j).
\]
  
As \(L\) was arbitrary, \(C\) is numerically equivalent to \([Z_0]_1\).

Finally, the connected group \(\mathbb C^{\times}\) cannot permute the finitely many components \(C_j\) nontrivially, so each of them is invariant. A component on which the action is trivial lies in the fixed locus, which is finite. Every other component contains a one-dimensional orbit, which is dense, so it is an orbit closure.

label: cor:nef-orbits
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:nef-orbits}
If the fixed locus is finite, a line bundle \(L\) on \(X\) is nef if and only if its degree is non-negative on every one-dimensional orbit closure.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: One implication is clear. Conversely, given a curve \(C\), write \(C\equiv\sum_jm_jC_j\) as in Proposition~\ref{prop:invariant-cycles}. Then \(L\cdot C=\sum_jm_j(L\cdot C_j)\geq0\), since each \(C_j\) is an orbit closure.

title: Definition
body_md:
The \emph{directed orbit graph} \(\Gamma(X)\) has vertex set \(X^{\mathbb C^{\times}}\). It has an edge \(p\to q\) when there is a non-fixed point \(x\in X\) with
  
\[
\lim_{t\to0}t\cdot x=p,
\qquad \lim_{t\to\infty}t\cdot x=q.
\]
  
A directed path of length \(r\) is a sequence of vertices \(p_0,\ldots,p_r\) with an edge \(p_{k-1}\to p_k\) for \(1\leq k\leq r\). An edge \(p\to q\) is \emph{minimal} if no path of length at least two has the same endpoints.
head: environment

label: lem:paths
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:paths}
Every directed edge can be replaced by a path consisting of minimal edges. Therefore, if every minimal edge has the form \(p_I\to p_{I\cup\{j\}}\), every edge \(p_I\to p_J\) satisfies \(I\subsetneq J\).
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Write \(p\leq q\) if \(p=q\) or there is a directed path from \(p\) to \(q\). Concatenation gives transitivity and the absence of cycles gives antisymmetry, so this is a partial order. If \(q\) covers \(p\), that is, \(p<q\) with no vertex strictly in between, then a path from \(p\) to \(q\) has no intermediate vertex, so it is a single edge, and that edge is minimal. Conversely, the endpoints of a minimal edge form a cover relation, since an intermediate vertex would give a longer path. Given \(p<q\), a chain between them of maximal length exists because the graph is finite, and its consecutive elements are cover relations, hence joined by minimal edges. Under the stated condition each of these edges adds one element to the label, so the initial label is strictly contained in the final one.
head: environment

label: prop:exact-criterion
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:exact-criterion}
All the Hattori line bundles are nef if and only if every edge \(p_I\to p_J\) of \(\Gamma(X)\) satisfies \(I\subsetneq J\).
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Suppose first that the line bundles are nef, and let \(C\) be an orbit closure for an edge \(p_I\to p_J\). If some \(i\) belonged to \(I\setminus J\), formula \eqref{eq:hattori-degree} would give \(L_i\cdot C=-1\). Hence \(I\subseteq J\), and \(I\ne J\) because the endpoints are distinct. Conversely, if every edge has nested labels, then by \eqref{eq:hattori-degree} each \(L_i\) has degree zero or one on every orbit closure, and Corollary~\ref{cor:nef-orbits} shows that it is nef.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Lemma~\ref{lem:paths}, every edge \(p_I\to p_J\) has \(I\subsetneq J\), so the \(L_i\) are nef by Proposition~\ref{prop:exact-criterion}. Together with Theorem~\ref{thm:htw}, this gives all the hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{thm:main}, and hence the product isomorphism of Proposition~\ref{prop:sections}.

To make it equivariant, give each \(L_i\) the linearisation of Lemma~\ref{lem:normalise-weights} and let \(\mathbb C^{\times}\) act on \(V_i=H^0(X,L_i)\) by
  
\[
(t\cdot s)(p)=t\cdot\bigl(s(t^{-1}\cdot p)\bigr),
\qquad t\in\mathbb C^{\times},\ s\in V_i,\ p\in X.
\]
  
At a fixed point, evaluation \(V_i\to(L_i)_p\) is equivariant, and it is surjective because \(L_i\) is globally generated. The fibre weights are zero at \(p_{\varnothing}\) and \(-1\) at \(p_{\{1,\ldots,n\}}\), so both weights occur in \(V_i\), and as \(\dim_{\mathbb C}V_i=2\) each occurs exactly once. Let \(s_{i,0}\) and \(s_{i,1}\) span the weight \(-1\) and weight zero subspaces, respectively. A section \(s\) of weight \(m\) satisfies
  
\[
s(t\cdot p)=t^{-m}\bigl(t\cdot s(p)\bigr),
\]
  
and in a local frame the action of \(t\) on the fibres multiplies both sections by the same factor, which cancels in homogeneous coordinates. Therefore
  
\[
[s_{i,0}(t\cdot p):s_{i,1}(t\cdot p)]
=[t s_{i,0}(p):s_{i,1}(p)],
\]
  
which is the required equivariance of the map in Proposition~\ref{prop:sections}.
